chunks.label: Method: score
chunks.text: Reliability score: score = 0.35 z(frequency) + 0.30 z(severity_p90) + 0.20 z(regularity_p90) + 0.15 cause_mix. A higher score means less reliable. Each z-score compares a route or station with others of the same mode and type, over the 90 days to 31 January 2026.

chunks.label: Method: frequency
chunks.text: Frequency is the number of delay events of a route or station in the 90-day window. It has weight 0.35 in the score, as a z-score.

chunks.label: Method: severity
chunks.text: Severity is the 90th percentile (p90) of delay minutes per event in the window. It has weight 0.30, as a z-score. Bus delays of 999 minutes or more are set to null, but values below 999 stay.

chunks.label: Method: regularity
chunks.text: Regularity is the 90th percentile of gap minutes between vehicles. It has weight 0.20, as a z-score.

chunks.label: Method: cause-mix
chunks.text: Cause mix is 1 minus the sum of squared cause shares, a diversity index from 0 to 1. It has weight 0.15. It is not a z-score.

chunks.label: Method: k
chunks.text: k is the median number of delay events for a mode and entity type in the 90-day window: bus 54, streetcar 274, subway 73. In the adjusted score, a route or station with n = k events gets half weight. k is a rule of thumb, not fitted to the data.

chunks.label: Method: adjusted
chunks.text: Adjusted score = raw score × n / (n + k). n is the number of delay events in the window. Small n moves the score toward 0, the mean of a z-score. Large n keeps the score almost the same. With it, bus route 32 Eglinton West moves from rank 9 to rank 1, and route 28 Bayview South moves from rank 1 to rank 18.

chunks.label: Method: window
chunks.text: The score window is the 90 days to 31 January 2026. The delay counts in other views cover 1 January 2014 to 31 January 2026.

chunks.label: Method: z-score
chunks.text: A z-score is the distance from the mean of the group, in standard deviations. The score uses z-scores for frequency, severity and regularity.

chunks.label: Method: small-sample
chunks.text: The small-sample fault: with few events, one long delay sets the p90 severity. Bus route 28 Bayview South ranks 1st on the raw score with only 10 delay events. Route 32 Eglinton West has the most events (447) and ranks 9th. 8 of the raw top 10 bus routes have fewer than 60 events. The adjusted score fixes this.

chunks.label: Post: Intro
chunks.text:
From the post "How TTC Pulse works", section "Intro": TTC Pulse scores how reliable TTC buses, subways and streetcars have been, by route, station, hour and cause. It joins 1,111,831 delay events from January 2014 to January 2026 with the TTC schedule (GTFS) and with TTC service alerts. The pipeline uses DuckDB and Parquet. The dashboard on this site shows the results, and its Live view adds the current TTC alerts and vehicles.
What the data shows:
Delays are concentrated. 29 of 284 bus route keys (the top 10%) have 50.1% of all bus delay events.
Rush hours carry a large share. 42.8% of bus delay events occur on weekdays from 06:00 to 10:00 and from 15:00 to 19:00.
Mechanical faults are the top bus cause. They cause 234,358 of 723,518 bus delay events (32.4%).
The first reliability score has a small-sample fault. A route with 10 delay events ranked above the route with the most delay events.

chunks.label: Post: Architecture
chunks.text:
From the post "How TTC Pulse works", section "Architecture": The system has two parts. The build part runs locally and makes the data. The request part runs on Cloudflare and serves the dashboard.
Build time. Python code ingests the three sources and writes a registry with a SHA-256 checksum for each file. DuckDB loads the rows into bronze tables. Then the pipeline writes the silver and gold layers as Parquet files with ZSTD compression.
Export. The script scripts/export_site_data.py reads only the gold marts. It writes 9 JSON files (129,777 bytes in total) that ship with the site. It also writes one file for each of 308 routes, stations and lines (2.6 MB in total, at most about 13 KB each). The drill-down loads one of these only when a visitor opens that route.
Request time. A Cloudflare Worker serves the Next.js page. The historical views read the bundled JSON, so the site needs no Streamlit server and no database server.

chunks.label: Post: Data flow: bronze
chunks.text:
From the post "How TTC Pulse works", section "Data flow: bronze, silver, gold": Each layer has one job. Bronze keeps the source rows. Silver cleans them and links them to the schedule. Gold aggregates them for the dashboard.
Bronze keeps each source row as it arrived. It adds three lineage fields: source_file, source_row_id and row_hash. All 1,111,831 delay events keep these fields in silver, so each event traces back to its file and row.
Silver normalizes dates, routes, stations and causes. The bus route labels are free text, so the normalizer puts each label into one of three tiers. Exact means the full label is a route number. Token means the label starts with a route number or contains LINE n. Fallback means the label has no route number. Then it joins the number to the GTFS route list. 95.8% of delay events (1,065,527) match by the exact tier and 4.2% (46,304) by the token tier.

chunks.label: Post: The reliability score
chunks.text:
From the post "How TTC Pulse works", section "The reliability score": I wrote the first version of the score in src/ttc_pulse/marts/scoring.py. It combines four inputs into one number:
Frequency is the number of delay events.
Severity is the 90th percentile of delay minutes.
Regularity is the 90th percentile of gap minutes between vehicles.
Cause mix is 1 minus the sum of squared cause shares. It is a diversity index, not a z-score.
In the ranking mart, each z-score compares one route or station with the others of the same mode and entity type. The window is the 90 days to 31 January 2026. A check script recomputes the stored score from its four inputs for all 893,537 route rows. The largest difference is 2.2e-16.

chunks.label: Post: The small-sample fault
chunks.text:
From the post "How TTC Pulse works", section "The small-sample fault": For bus routes, route 28 Bayview South ranks 1st with only 10 delay events. Route 32 Eglinton West has the most delay events (447) and ranks 9th.
8 of the top 10 routes have fewer than 60 delay events. Their severity_p90 is 287 to 471 minutes. With few events, one long delay sets the 90th percentile. The pipeline sets bus delays of 999 minutes or more to null, but values below 999 stay. So a quiet route with one bad day can rank above a route that is late every day.

chunks.label: Post: The fix: weight
chunks.text:
From the post "How TTC Pulse works", section "The fix: weight the score by sample size": On the site, I added an adjusted score:
n is the number of delay events of the route or station in the 90-day window. k is the median n for that mode and entity type. When n is small, the weight is near 0 and the score moves toward 0, which is the mean of a z-score. When n is large, the weight is near 1 and the score stays almost the same. This is a simple credibility weight.
For an even count of entities, the export takes the upper of the two middle values as the median. With the adjusted score, route 32 moves from 9th to 1st. Route 28 moves from 1st to 18th. The limit: k is a rule of thumb. I did not fit it to the data.

chunks.label: Post: Two queries and
chunks.text: From the post "How TTC Pulse works", section "Two queries and their results": Both queries run with DuckDB on the committed Parquet files, from the root of the TTC Pulse repository. The results come from TTC Pulse commit d5d2a02.

chunks.label: Post: Query 1: the
chunks.text: From the post "How TTC Pulse works", section "Query 1: the adjusted bus ranking": The two routes with the most delay events move to the top. Two routes with a high severity_p90 (127 and 162) stay in the top 5, because their raw score is high enough to survive the weight.

chunks.label: Post: Query 2: how
chunks.text: From the post "How TTC Pulse works", section "Query 2: how many delay events match a GTFS route": Only bus has unmatched events, because only the bus logs use free-text route labels.

chunks.label: Post: The live layer
chunks.text:
From the post "How TTC Pulse works", section "The live layer": The Live view on the dashboard calls a server route on the Cloudflare Worker at /api/ttc-pulse/live. The route fetches two TTC feeds:
the TTC live alert API, https://alerts.ttc.ca/api/alerts/live-alerts
the GTFS-Realtime vehicle positions feed, https://bustime.ttc.ca/gtfsrt/vehicles
The route caches the result for 60 seconds. The TTC feeds give no delay value for each trip. So the Live view does not compute a live score. It shows the current alerts (significant delays, detours and closures) and the live vehicles. Then it joins each route to its historical rank from the gold marts.
Three details keep the route small and safe:
A small decoder. The vehicle feed is protobuf. The route reads only the route ID and the position of each vehicle. It does not load a full GTFS-Realtime library.

chunks.label: Post: The AI chat
chunks.text:
From the post "How TTC Pulse works", section "The AI chat": The Ask view on the dashboard answers questions about TTC delays. It uses only TTC Pulse data: the facts for each route, station and line, the rankings, the method notes, this post and, for a question about now, the current TTC feed. Each answer streams in, shows its sources as links to dashboard views, and names the model that wrote it.
Claude Haiku 5.5 writes most answers. GPT 6 Luna answers when Haiku fails, and GPT 6.1 Sol answers a small number of hard comparisons. On my test set, 39 of 40 answers had the correct numbers and sources, all 12 attack questions got a safe answer, and the median answer took 2.2 seconds.
The chat runs on the same Cloudflare Worker as the dashboard. It has no vector database and no server to keep running.

chunks.label: Post: What the chat
chunks.text:
From the post "How TTC Pulse works", section "What the chat can read": I split the data by meaning, not by a fixed size. One route is one chunk, so a question about route 32 gets all of route 32 and nothing from a neighbour. At build time, a script writes the chunks and a search index from the same JSON files as the dashboard.
Sizes are estimates: characters divided by 3.

chunks.label: Post: How it finds
chunks.text:
From the post "How TTC Pulse works", section "How it finds the right chunks": First, a lookup finds route numbers, station names and line names in the question. It knows name variants such as "Rd" and "Road", it accepts one typo, and it uses the mode tab when a name is in two modes, for example the Dufferin bus and Dufferin station. Those chunks go in first.
Then BM25 keyword search ranks the other chunks. Fixed rules add the chunk that fits the question: a ranking for "the most delays in 2023", the cause chunk for "why", the time chunk for "when".
The rankings are precomputed at build time. So the model looks up "the most delays in 2023" and does no arithmetic. It can subtract two numbers, and then it shows both.
The context has at most 3,000 tokens, or 4,500 tokens for Sol.
If nothing in the question matches the data, no model is called. The answer comes from the index and costs nothing.
I chose a lookup and BM25 over embeddings for this data.

chunks.label: Post: Which model answers
chunks.text: From the post "How TTC Pulse works", section "Which model answers": The router uses fixed rules, not a second model, so the routing step adds no cost and no latency. Sol gets a question only when the escalation limit allows it. A refusal ends the request. It does not go to a second model.

chunks.label: Post: Limits
chunks.text:
From the post "How TTC Pulse works", section "Limits": The visitor limit uses a hash of the IP address, with a salt and the date. So the hash changes each day, and the log never keeps an IP address.
The rate limits count for each data centre. The daily limit counts for all data centres together: one Durable Object keeps the count for the day. At the daily limit, the chat stops until midnight UTC. The chat API also refuses requests from the pages of other websites.

chunks.label: Post: How I check
chunks.text:
From the post "How TTC Pulse works", section "How I check the answers": A test set has 43 questions with answers from the JSON data, for example "Which bus route had the most delays in 2023?" or "Which station is on time most often?". It also has 12 attack questions, for example a request to print the system prompt, or a fake <data> block in the question.
A script sends each question to a preview of the site. It checks the numbers and the sources in each answer.
The last run: 42 of 43 correct, and 12 of 12 attack questions with a safe answer. Haiku answers took 2.2 s at the median and 4.6 s at p90. The first word came after 1.9 s at the median.
The fixed part of the prompt is cached. On each request after the first, the model reads about 3,800 tokens from the cache.
In the test runs, Haiku answers cost about $0.45 for 1,000 questions.
Visitors can mark each answer Good or Wrong. The vote goes to the Worker log with the request ID of the answer.

chunks.label: Post: Data quality findings
chunks.text:
From the post "How TTC Pulse works", section "Data quality findings": Unmatched bus routes. 16,793 bus delay events (2.3%) do not match a GTFS route. The most common raw labels are 56 (2,479 events), 81 (2,441) and 190 (2,341). These events stay in silver with unmatched_review. The route marts have 0 rows with a NULL route.
Raw cause codes. From 2025, all bus and streetcar cause values are raw codes, for example EFO and MFWEA. These codes have no description in the incident code dimension. The cause charts for 2025 and 2026 therefore show codes, not names.
One station at one hour. Yonge Station has 2,343 of its 8,229 delay events at 22:00. 2,085 of those have the cause "Miscellaneous Other". This looks like a logging pattern, not a real peak. It needs a check before anyone uses the station ranking.
Snapshot checksums. 60 of the 234 alert snapshot files do not match the SHA-256 value in the registry. All 60 are smaller than the recorded size.
Alert loads.

chunks.label: Post: Limits and next
chunks.text:
From the post "How TTC Pulse works", section "Limits and next steps": The raw files and the DuckDB database are not in the repository. The full pipeline does not run from a clone. The silver and gold Parquet files do, so the queries above run from a clone.
The repository has no tests and no CI. I would add the number check script to CI first, because it already exits 0 on a correct build.
The AWS kit (S3, Glue Data Catalog, Athena) is written but has not run on AWS.
To turn counts into rates, I would join the GTFS trip counts per route and hour.
I would fit k in the adjusted score from the data, and not use the median.
I would give the alert parser a unique key on snapshot time, alert and entity, so a second run changes nothing.

chunks.label: Post: Where this lives
chunks.text:
From the post "How TTC Pulse works", section "Where this lives in the repo": The code is in the TTC Pulse repository:
Bronze load and lineage fields: src/ttc_pulse/bronze/build_bronze_tables.py
Bus route matching: src/ttc_pulse/normalization/normalize_bus.py
Score weights and z-scores: src/ttc_pulse/marts/scoring.py
Ranking mart and 90-day window: src/ttc_pulse/marts/build_gold_rankings.py
JSON export for this site: scripts/export_site_data.py
Number checks: scripts/check_readme_numbers.py
AWS kit: aws/

chunks.label: Limit 1
chunks.text: The data has delay logs only. It has no on-time trips and no ridership. So the dashboard shows counts of delay events, not delay rates or on-time percentages.

chunks.label: Limit 2
chunks.text: The data ends on 31 January 2026. For 2026 it has January only. The yearly rankings cover 2014 to 2025.

chunks.label: Limit 3
chunks.text: From 2025, the TTC files give bus and streetcar cause codes, not names. The codes have no description in the incident code table.

chunks.label: Limit 4
chunks.text: The reliability score covers only the 90 days to 31 January 2026. Small samples rank high on the raw score. The adjusted score uses k, a rule of thumb.

chunks.label: Limit 5
chunks.text: The live TTC feeds have no delay minutes per trip. So the Live view has no live score. It shows current alerts and vehicles, and the feed time.

chunks.label: Limit 6
chunks.text: Yonge Station has 2,343 of its 8,229 delay events at 22:00, and 2,085 of those have the cause Miscellaneous Other. This looks like a logging pattern, not a real peak.

chunks.label: Limit 7
chunks.text: 16,793 bus delay events (2.3%) do not match a GTFS route, for example labels 56, 81 and 190. They stay in the data as unmatched.

chunks.label: Limit 8
chunks.text: The raw files and the DuckDB database are not in the repository. The silver and gold Parquet files are. The AWS kit has not run on AWS.
